history.q: Which family's shogunate ruled Japan from 1603 to 1868?
history.fact: The Tokugawa shoguns governed from Edo, a fishing village they turned into one of the world's largest cities; today we know it as Tokyo.

history.q: Which US naval commander arrived with his 'Black Ships' in 1853 to press Japan to open its ports?
history.fact: Perry returned in 1854 to sign the Convention of Kanagawa, which opened the ports of Shimoda and Hakodate to American ships.

history.q: Heian-kyo, founded as Japan's capital in 794, is known today as which city?
history.fact: Kyoto remained the imperial capital for more than 1,000 years, until the Emperor moved to Tokyo in 1869.

history.q: The word 'kamikaze' (divine wind) first referred to typhoons said to have wrecked invasion fleets of which empire?
history.fact: The Mongols under Kublai Khan attempted to invade Japan twice, in 1274 and 1281, and storms battered their fleets both times.

history.q: In which year did the Meiji Restoration return power from the shogun to the Emperor?
history.fact: During the Meiji Restoration, Edo was renamed Tokyo, meaning 'Eastern Capital', and became the Emperor's new home.

history.q: Victory in which battle of 1600 paved the way for Tokugawa Ieyasu to become shogun?
history.fact: Sekigahara is often called the most decisive battle in Japanese history; three years later, in 1603, Ieyasu was appointed shogun.

history.q: Who founded the Kamakura shogunate, Japan's first shogunate, in the late 12th century?
history.fact: The Kamakura shogunate began an era of warrior rule that, in one form or another, lasted almost 700 years until 1868.

history.q: Which warlord began unifying Japan in the 16th century but died in the Honno-ji Incident of 1582?
history.fact: Oda Nobunaga was betrayed by his own general, Akechi Mitsuhide, at Honno-ji temple in Kyoto; Toyotomi Hideyoshi went on to complete unification.

history.q: What name is given to the Tokugawa policy that sharply restricted foreign contact, allowing only limited trade such as with the Dutch and Chinese at Nagasaki?
history.fact: From 1641 Dutch traders were confined to Dejima, a small fan-shaped artificial island in Nagasaki harbour.

history.q: In which year did the Treaty of Portsmouth end the Russo-Japanese War?
history.fact: US President Theodore Roosevelt brokered the Treaty of Portsmouth and won the 1906 Nobel Peace Prize for his efforts.

history.q: Which Japanese city was the first to be struck by an atomic bomb, on 6 August 1945?
history.fact: The Genbaku Dome, one of the few buildings left standing near the blast's centre, is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site and peace memorial.

history.q: On 7 December 1941, Japan launched a surprise attack on which US naval base?
history.fact: The attacking planes flew from six aircraft carriers; a memorial now stands over the sunken battleship USS Arizona.

history.q: What was the name of Japan's hereditary warrior class?
history.fact: The samurai lost their privileges in the Meiji reforms of the 1870s, and a decree of 1876 banned the wearing of swords in public.

history.q: Which emperor reigned over Japan during World War II?
history.fact: Hirohito reigned from 1926 to 1989, the longest reign of any Japanese emperor in recorded history; his era is known as Showa.

history.q: Aboard which US battleship did Japan sign its formal surrender in September 1945?
history.fact: The ceremony took place in Tokyo Bay on 2 September 1945; the Missouri is now a museum ship at Pearl Harbor.

history.q: Which city, founded as Japan's capital in 710, is home to the giant bronze Buddha of Todai-ji?
history.fact: Nara's deer, long regarded as sacred messengers of the gods, roam freely through the city's parks and bow to visitors for special crackers.

history.q: Which war of 1894-95 gave Japan control of Taiwan?
history.fact: Under the Treaty of Shimonoseki that ended the war, China ceded Taiwan to Japan and recognised Korea's independence.

history.q: Which 1877 uprising, led by Saigo Takamori, was the last major samurai rebellion?
history.fact: A famous bronze statue of Saigo Takamori walking his dog stands in Tokyo's Ueno Park.

history.q: In which battle of June 1942 did Japan lose four aircraft carriers, a turning point of the Pacific War?
history.fact: US codebreakers had partly cracked Japan's naval code, giving the US Navy warning that Midway was the target.

history.q: What name is given to Japan's 'Warring States' era of near-constant civil war in the 15th and 16th centuries?
history.fact: During the Sengoku period, in 1543, Portuguese traders landed on Tanegashima island and introduced the first firearms to Japan.

history.q: Which 1637-38 uprising of largely Christian peasants in Kyushu led to tighter bans on Christianity?
history.fact: The rebels were led by Amakusa Shiro, a charismatic teenager; their stronghold at Hara Castle held out for months before it fell.

history.q: Which Jesuit missionary brought Christianity to Japan in 1549?
history.fact: Francis Xavier landed at Kagoshima in 1549 and spent about two years in Japan before leaving to plan a mission to China.

history.q: What was the name of the 1868-69 civil war between shogunate forces and supporters of imperial rule?
history.fact: The war's last stand came at Goryokaku, a star-shaped fort in Hakodate, where shogunate loyalists had declared a short-lived Republic of Ezo.

history.q: Which 1180-1185 conflict ended with the naval Battle of Dan-no-ura?
history.fact: At Dan-no-ura in 1185 the child emperor Antoku drowned; the story is retold in the epic 'Tale of the Heike'.

history.q: Which Meiji-era slogan, meaning 'rich country, strong army', guided Japan's modernisation?
history.fact: As part of the push for a strong army, Japan introduced universal male conscription in 1873.

technology.q: Japan's first Shinkansen bullet train line, opened in 1964, linked Tokyo with which city?
technology.fact: The Tokaido Shinkansen opened on 1 October 1964, just nine days before the opening ceremony of the Tokyo Olympics.

technology.q: Which company launched the Walkman portable cassette player in 1979?
technology.fact: The first Walkman had two headphone jacks so that two people could listen together.

technology.q: Which carmaker developed the 'just-in-time' lean production system studied by factories worldwide?
technology.fact: Toyota also launched the Prius in 1997, the world's first mass-produced hybrid car.

technology.q: Which Kyoto company, founded in 1889 as a maker of playing cards, later released the Game Boy?
technology.fact: Nintendo started out making hanafuda, colourful Japanese flower cards, and still sells them today.

technology.q: The QR code was invented in Japan in 1994. What was it originally designed to track?
technology.fact: QR stands for 'Quick Response'. Engineer Masahiro Hara of Denso Wave designed it to be read far faster than a traditional barcode.

technology.q: Shinya Yamanaka shared the 2012 Nobel Prize for showing that adult cells can be reprogrammed into what?
technology.fact: Yamanaka shared the prize with Britain's John Gurdon; his 'iPS cells' can develop into almost any type of cell in the body.

technology.q: Isamu Akasaki, Hiroshi Amano and Shuji Nakamura won the 2014 Nobel Prize in Physics for efficient LEDs of which colour?
technology.fact: Blue LEDs were the missing piece needed to make bright, energy-saving white LED light, now used in lamps and screens everywhere.

technology.q: In 2010, Japan's Hayabusa probe became the first spacecraft to return samples from what?
technology.fact: Despite engine failures and a lost lander, Hayabusa limped home in June 2010 carrying tiny grains from the asteroid Itokawa.

technology.q: Which Japanese bridge held the world record for the longest suspension span from 1998 until 2022?
technology.fact: The Akashi Kaikyo Bridge's central span is 1,991 metres long; it links Kobe with Awaji Island across a busy, storm-prone strait.

technology.q: Shigetaka Kurita designed one of the first widely used emoji sets in 1999 for which mobile internet service?
technology.fact: Kurita's original set of 176 emoji, each just 12 by 12 pixels, was added to the collection of New York's Museum of Modern Art in 2016.

technology.q: Which games console did Sony first release in Japan in December 1994?
technology.fact: The PlayStation grew out of a cancelled CD-ROM add-on that Sony had been developing with Nintendo for the Super Nintendo.

technology.q: Which Nintendo designer created Super Mario and The Legend of Zelda?
technology.fact: Mario first appeared in the 1981 arcade game Donkey Kong, where he was simply called 'Jumpman'.

technology.q: What did Momofuku Ando invent in Japan in 1958?
technology.fact: Ando's first product, Chicken Ramen, was flash-fried to dry it; he went on to launch Cup Noodles in 1971.

technology.q: Which Japanese carmaker produces the Civic and the Accord?
technology.fact: Soichiro Honda started out fitting small engines to bicycles after World War II; by 1959 Honda was the world's largest motorcycle maker.

technology.q: What is the name of Japan's national space agency?
technology.fact: JAXA was formed in 2003 by merging three organisations, including the Institute of Space and Astronautical Science (ISAS).

technology.q: Which Japanese electronics giant was founded by Konosuke Matsushita in Osaka in 1918?
technology.fact: Matsushita's first hit product was an improved two-way light socket, and he became known in Japan as the 'god of management'.

technology.q: Who became Japan's first Nobel laureate, winning the Physics prize in 1949?
technology.fact: Yukawa predicted the meson, a particle carrying the strong nuclear force, in 1935; it was detected in cosmic rays in 1947.

technology.q: Which Japanese company sold the world's first quartz wristwatch, the Astron, in 1969?
technology.fact: The Seiko Quartz Astron went on sale on Christmas Day 1969 and cost about as much as a small car.

technology.q: What is the name of Japan's laboratory module on the International Space Station?
technology.fact: Kibo means 'hope' and is the largest single module on the ISS; it even has an outdoor platform for experiments exposed to space.

technology.q: Which bacteriologist, pictured on Japan's 1,000-yen note from 2004, researched yellow fever?
technology.fact: Hideyo Noguchi died of yellow fever in Accra, in present-day Ghana, in 1928 while studying the disease.

technology.q: Which Japanese bacteriologist worked with Emil von Behring on serum therapy for tetanus and diphtheria?
technology.fact: Kitasato founded the institute that grew into Kitasato University, and in 2024 his portrait appeared on Japan's new 1,000-yen note.

technology.q: Hidetsugu Yagi and Shintaro Uda are known for inventing what in 1926?
technology.fact: The Yagi-Uda antenna drew little attention in Japan at first but was widely used for radar in World War II and later for rooftop TV reception.

technology.q: Which engineer is called the 'father of Japanese television' for displaying an image electronically on a cathode-ray tube in 1926?
technology.fact: Takayanagi's first electronically displayed image was the katakana character 'i' (イ), shown in December 1926.

technology.q: Akira Yoshino shared the 2019 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for developing which technology?
technology.fact: Yoshino, who worked for the chemicals company Asahi Kasei, shared the prize with John Goodenough and Stanley Whittingham.

technology.q: In 2015, a Japanese superconducting maglev test train set the world speed record for a rail vehicle. How fast did it go?
technology.fact: The record was set on the Yamanashi test line, part of the planned Chuo Shinkansen maglev route between Tokyo and Nagoya.

art.q: Which artist created the woodblock print 'The Great Wave off Kanagawa'?
art.fact: The Great Wave, made around 1831, is part of the series 'Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji'; look closely and you'll spot Fuji in the trough of the wave.

art.q: Which Hayao Miyazaki film became the first anime to win the Oscar for Best Animated Feature?
art.fact: Spirited Away also shared the Golden Bear at the 2002 Berlin Film Festival, a rare honour for an animated film.

art.q: Who directed the 1954 film 'Seven Samurai'?
art.fact: Seven Samurai was remade in Hollywood as the western 'The Magnificent Seven' (1960).

art.q: Which poet wrote the famous haiku about a frog leaping into an old pond?
art.fact: Basho also wrote 'The Narrow Road to the Deep North', a travel journal mixing prose and haiku from his long walk through northern Japan.

art.q: Who wrote 'The Tale of Genji', the classic of the Heian court written in the early 11th century?
art.fact: The Tale of Genji is often called the world's first novel; its author was a lady-in-waiting at the imperial court in Kyoto.

art.q: Which theatre form, said to have been started by a woman named Izumo no Okuni around 1603, is now performed by all-male casts?
art.fact: Women were banned from the kabuki stage in 1629, giving rise to the onnagata, male actors who specialise in female roles.

art.q: What is Japan's traditional puppet theatre, in which each main puppet is worked by three puppeteers?
art.fact: Many of Japan's most celebrated plays were written for the puppet stage by Chikamatsu Monzaemon, often called 'Japan's Shakespeare'.

art.q: Who became the first Japanese writer to win the Nobel Prize in Literature, in 1968?
art.fact: Kawabata was honoured for novels such as 'Snow Country'; Kenzaburo Oe became Japan's second literature laureate in 1994.

art.q: Which ukiyo-e artist created the print series 'The Fifty-three Stations of the Tokaido'?
art.fact: Vincent van Gogh admired Hiroshige so much that he painted his own copies of two of Hiroshige's prints.

art.q: Which 16th-century master shaped the Japanese tea ceremony around the rustic ideal of 'wabi'?
art.fact: Sen no Rikyu served as tea master to Oda Nobunaga and Toyotomi Hideyoshi, who ordered him to commit ritual suicide in 1591.

art.q: Which giant monster first stomped through Tokyo in a 1954 film?
art.fact: Godzilla's Japanese name, Gojira, blends gorira (gorilla) and kujira (whale).

art.q: What is the Japanese art of paper folding called?
art.fact: The crane is the classic origami model; strings of 1,000 paper cranes, called senbazuru, are folded as wishes for luck or recovery.

art.q: Which novelist wrote 'Norwegian Wood' and 'Kafka on the Shore'?
art.fact: Haruki Murakami ran a jazz bar in Tokyo before becoming a writer; 'Norwegian Wood' takes its title from a Beatles song.

art.q: Which animation studio, co-founded by Hayao Miyazaki in 1985, made 'My Neighbor Totoro'?
art.fact: Totoro, the friendly forest spirit from the 1988 film, became Studio Ghibli's logo.

art.q: Which manga and anime series follows Goku and the quest for seven magic balls?
art.fact: Dragon Ball's creator Akira Toriyama loosely based it on Journey to the West; Son Goku is the Japanese reading of Sun Wukong.

art.q: What is the Japanese art of mending broken pottery with lacquer dusted with gold?
art.fact: Kintsugi treats breakage as part of an object's history; legend links it to shogun Ashikaga Yoshimasa, who disliked a crude metal-staple repair.

art.q: Which novelist wrote 'The Temple of the Golden Pavilion' and died after a failed coup attempt in 1970?
art.fact: The novel is based on the real 1950 arson of Kyoto's Kinkaku-ji by a young monk; the temple was rebuilt in 1955.

art.q: Which self-taught architect, a former boxer, designed Osaka's Church of the Light?
art.fact: Tadao Ando won the Pritzker Prize in 1995; the cross in the Church of the Light is formed by slits cut into a concrete wall.

art.q: Which composer has written the music for most of Hayao Miyazaki's films?
art.fact: Joe Hisaishi's stage name is a tribute to Quincy Jones: 'Hisaishi' comes from a Japanese reading of 'Quincy', and 'Joe' from 'Jones'.

art.q: Which Japanese musician shared the Oscar for Best Original Score for 'The Last Emperor' (1987)?
art.fact: Sakamoto was a founding member of Yellow Magic Orchestra, the Tokyo band whose synth-pop helped shape electronic music.

art.q: Which architect designed the Yoyogi National Gymnasium for the 1964 Tokyo Olympics?
art.fact: Kenzo Tange won the Pritzker Prize in 1987, the first Japanese architect to receive it.

art.q: Which director made 'Tokyo Story' (1953)?
art.fact: In 2012, a Sight and Sound poll of film directors voted Tokyo Story the greatest film ever made.

art.q: Which masked dance-drama was perfected by Zeami in the 14th and 15th centuries?
art.fact: Zeami and his father Kan'ami developed Noh under the patronage of shogun Ashikaga Yoshimitsu, builder of Kyoto's Golden Pavilion.

art.q: Which Heian-era court lady wrote 'The Pillow Book'?
art.fact: The Pillow Book is full of lists, such as 'Things That Make One's Heart Beat Faster'; its author served Empress Teishi around the year 1000.

art.q: Which ukiyo-e master is best known for close-up portraits of beautiful women (bijin-ga)?
art.fact: In 1804 Utamaro was handcuffed for 50 days as punishment for prints depicting the warlord Toyotomi Hideyoshi, a banned subject.

politics.q: What is the name of Japan's national legislature?
politics.fact: Japan's first Diet convened in 1890 under the Meiji Constitution; today's Diet Building in Tokyo's Nagatacho district was completed in 1936.

politics.q: Under Japan's 1947 constitution, how is the Emperor defined?
choices: As the symbol of the State and the unity of the people
politics.fact: Japan's imperial line is traditionally regarded as the oldest continuous hereditary monarchy in the world.

politics.q: Who is Japan's longest-serving prime minister?
politics.fact: Shinzo Abe served two stints, in 2006-07 and 2012-20; his economic programme became known as 'Abenomics'.

politics.q: Which party has governed Japan for most of the period since its founding in 1955?
politics.fact: Since its creation through a merger in 1955, the LDP has been out of power only twice: in 1993-94 and 2009-12.

politics.q: Which article of Japan's 1947 constitution renounces war as a sovereign right of the nation?
politics.fact: The constitution took effect on 3 May 1947, a date still marked each year as Constitution Memorial Day, a national holiday.

politics.q: Who became Japan's first prime minister in 1885?
politics.fact: Ito Hirobumi served as prime minister four times, and his portrait appeared on the 1,000-yen note first issued in 1963.

politics.q: In which year was the Meiji Constitution, Japan's first modern constitution, promulgated?
politics.fact: The Meiji Constitution drew heavily on the Prussian model, which Ito Hirobumi had studied in Europe.

politics.q: What is the upper house of Japan's National Diet called?
politics.fact: Members of the House of Councillors serve six-year terms, with half of the seats up for election every three years.

politics.q: Which regent is traditionally credited with Japan's Seventeen-Article Constitution of 604 CE?
politics.fact: The Seventeen-Article Constitution was a moral code for officials rather than a legal constitution; its first article praises harmony (wa).

politics.q: Which prime minister signed the 1951 San Francisco Peace Treaty for Japan?
politics.fact: The San Francisco Peace Treaty took effect on 28 April 1952, formally ending the Allied occupation of Japan.

politics.q: Which Emperor of Japan abdicated in 2019, the first to step down in about two centuries?
politics.fact: The previous abdication was by Emperor Kokaku in 1817; a special law had to be passed in 2017 to allow Akihito to step down.

politics.q: Which American general led the Allied occupation of Japan after World War II?
politics.fact: In February 1946 MacArthur's staff drafted much of Japan's postwar constitution in little more than a week.

politics.q: What are Japan's armed forces, established in 1954, called?
politics.fact: The Self-Defense Forces grew out of the National Police Reserve, created in 1950 during the Korean War.

politics.q: Which flower appears on the Imperial Seal of Japan?
politics.fact: The government of Japan uses a different emblem, the paulownia (kiri) crest, which appears on official documents and the prime minister's lectern.

politics.q: Japan is a member of which group of seven major industrialised democracies?
politics.fact: Japan has hosted the G7 summit seven times, most recently in Hiroshima in 2023.

politics.q: Who became the first woman elected Governor of Tokyo, in 2016?
politics.fact: Before entering politics Yuriko Koike was a TV news anchor, and in 2007 she became Japan's first female Minister of Defence.

politics.q: Which prime minister of 2001-2006 championed the privatisation of Japan Post?
politics.fact: Koizumi called a snap election over postal privatisation in 2005 and won a landslide; he is also a famous fan of Elvis Presley.

politics.q: Which Japanese prime minister shared the 1974 Nobel Peace Prize?
politics.fact: Sato was honoured largely for his non-nuclear policy; his elder brother, Nobusuke Kishi, had also been prime minister.

politics.q: Which islands were returned to Japanese administration by the United States in 1972?
politics.fact: Okinawa switched from driving on the right to the left in 1978 in a one-night changeover known as '730', after its date, 30 July.

politics.q: Who was Japan's prime minister at the time of the attack on Pearl Harbor?
politics.fact: Tojo was also War Minister; after the war he was tried by the International Military Tribunal for the Far East and executed in 1948.

politics.q: Which prime minister normalised Japan's diplomatic relations with the People's Republic of China in 1972?
politics.fact: To mark the occasion, China sent two giant pandas, Kang Kang and Lan Lan, to Tokyo's Ueno Zoo in 1972.

politics.q: Which Japanese diplomatic mission of 1871-73 toured the United States and Europe to study Western institutions?
politics.fact: The mission took five young girls to study in the US, among them Tsuda Umeko, who later founded what is now Tsuda University.

politics.q: In which year did Japan join the United Nations?
politics.fact: Japan's admission followed a joint declaration that restored diplomatic relations with the Soviet Union, which had previously blocked its membership.

politics.q: Who was Japan's prime minister at the time of the March 2011 earthquake and Fukushima nuclear disaster?
politics.fact: The Democratic Party of Japan governed from 2009 to 2012 with three prime ministers: Yukio Hatoyama, Naoto Kan and Yoshihiko Noda.

politics.q: What is the Japanese prime minister's official office in Tokyo commonly called?
politics.fact: The current Kantei opened in 2002; the original 1929 building next door was moved and converted into the prime minister's residence.

current-affairs.q: Which city hosted the Summer Olympics held in 2021?
current-affairs.fact: Postponed by a year because of COVID-19, the Games kept the name 'Tokyo 2020' and were held almost entirely without spectators.

current-affairs.q: What era name (gengo) began in Japan when Emperor Naruhito acceded to the throne in May 2019?
current-affairs.fact: Reiwa was taken from the Man'yoshu poetry anthology, the first era name drawn from Japanese rather than Chinese classical literature.

current-affairs.q: Which Japanese city hosted the World Expo held in 2025?
current-affairs.fact: Expo 2025 was held on Yumeshima, an artificial island; its 'Grand Ring' was certified as the world's largest wooden architectural structure.

current-affairs.q: Which Japanese baseball star signed a 10-year, $700 million contract with the Los Angeles Dodgers in December 2023?
current-affairs.fact: In 2024 Shohei Ohtani became the first Major League player to hit 50 home runs and steal 50 bases in a single season.

current-affairs.q: Who became Prime Minister of Japan in October 2024 after winning the LDP leadership?
current-affairs.fact: Shigeru Ishiba won the LDP leadership in 2024 on his fifth attempt, having previously run in 2008, 2012, 2018 and 2020.

current-affairs.q: In October 2025, who became Japan's first female Prime Minister?
current-affairs.fact: Sanae Takaichi, a former Minister for Internal Affairs and Communications, has often named Margaret Thatcher as a political role model.

current-affairs.q: Japan's SLIM lander touched down in January 2024. Which country in order did that make Japan to soft-land on the Moon?
current-affairs.fact: Nicknamed the 'Moon Sniper', SLIM touched down within about 100 metres of its target, although it ended up resting on its nose.

current-affairs.q: Which Japanese city, together with its home prefecture, hosted the Asian Games that ended on 4 October 2026?
current-affairs.fact: The Aichi-Nagoya Games were Japan's third summer Asian Games after Tokyo 1958 and Hiroshima 1994. Japan won a record 269 medals, including 83 golds, finishing second to China.

current-affairs.q: In December 2020, Japan's Hayabusa2 mission delivered samples to Earth from which asteroid?
current-affairs.fact: Hayabusa2's sample capsule parachuted into the Australian outback, and scientists later found amino acids in the Ryugu material.

current-affairs.q: Which industrialist, known as the 'father of Japanese capitalism', appears on the new 10,000-yen note issued in 2024?
current-affairs.fact: The new 1,000-yen note issued in 2024 features Hokusai's 'Great Wave off Kanagawa' on its reverse.

current-affairs.q: Which former prime minister was assassinated while giving a campaign speech in Nara in July 2022?
current-affairs.fact: Abe was given a state funeral in Tokyo in September 2022, the first for a former prime minister since Shigeru Yoshida's in 1967.

current-affairs.q: Which Japanese player won the women's singles title at the 2021 Australian Open?
current-affairs.fact: Naomi Osaka lit the Olympic cauldron at the Tokyo Games in 2021; she has won four Grand Slam singles titles.

current-affairs.q: Which country did Japan beat in the final of the 2023 World Baseball Classic?
current-affairs.fact: The final ended with Shohei Ohtani striking out his Angels teammate Mike Trout, and Ohtani was named the tournament's MVP.

current-affairs.q: Which Japanese monster film won the Oscar for Best Visual Effects in 2024?
current-affairs.fact: Director Takashi Yamazaki also supervised the film's visual effects, and accepted the award with his team.

current-affairs.q: Which Hayao Miyazaki film won the Oscar for Best Animated Feature in 2024?
current-affairs.fact: The film's Japanese title, 'How Do You Live?', comes from a 1937 novel by Genzaburo Yoshino that Miyazaki loved as a boy.

current-affairs.q: Which Japanese prime minister hosted the G7 summit in his home constituency of Hiroshima in May 2023?
current-affairs.fact: As a boy Fumio Kishida lived in New York, where his father was posted, and attended a public elementary school in Queens.

current-affairs.q: In 2021, which golfer became the first Japanese man to win the Masters?
current-affairs.fact: After Matsuyama's win, his caddie Shota Hayafuji replaced the flag on the 18th green and bowed to the course, a gesture admired worldwide.

current-affairs.q: In August 2023 Japan began releasing treated water into the sea from which nuclear power plant?
current-affairs.fact: The treated water is diluted with seawater and released through an undersea tunnel about one kilometre offshore.

current-affairs.q: Which city hosted the World Athletics Championships held in September 2025?
current-affairs.fact: Tokyo had hosted the championships once before, in 1991, when Mike Powell set a long-jump world record of 8.95 metres.

current-affairs.q: In the February 2026 general election, Sanae Takaichi's party set a postwar record for seats won by a single party. Which party is it?
current-affairs.fact: The LDP won 316 of 465 seats, beating the Democratic Party of Japan's 308 in 2009 and the LDP's own 300 in 1986. With its coalition partner it held about three-quarters of the lower house.

current-affairs.q: Who won the men's individual all-around gymnastics gold at the Paris 2024 Olympics?
current-affairs.fact: Shinnosuke Oka won three golds in Paris, in the all-around, team and horizontal bar events, keeping the all-around title in Japanese hands.

current-affairs.q: What is the name of Japan's new flagship rocket, which first reached orbit in February 2024?
current-affairs.fact: The H3's first launch in March 2023 failed when its second stage did not ignite, so the February 2024 success was a big relief for JAXA.

current-affairs.q: Which Japanese organisation of atomic bomb survivors won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2024?
current-affairs.fact: Nihon Hidankyo was founded in 1956 by hibakusha, survivors of the Hiroshima and Nagasaki bombings.

current-affairs.q: Which wrestler was promoted to sumo's top rank of yokozuna in May 2025, the first Japanese-born yokozuna since 2017?
current-affairs.fact: Onosato reached yokozuna just 13 tournaments after his professional debut in 2023, the fastest rise to sumo's top rank of the modern era.

current-affairs.q: In March 2024 the Bank of Japan ended a policy it had kept since 2016. What was it?
current-affairs.fact: The move was the Bank of Japan's first interest rate rise in 17 years.

society.q: In October 2019, Japan raised its consumption tax from 8% to what rate?
society.fact: Food and non-alcoholic drinks kept a reduced 8% rate, so a takeaway meal is taxed less than the same meal eaten in; the rise had been delayed twice since 2015.

society.q: Japan's population has fallen every year since peaking in 2008. Roughly what was it in 2024?
society.fact: The number of Japanese nationals fell by a record of roughly 900,000 in 2024, while the number of foreign residents rose to a record high.

society.q: In 2024, annual births in Japan fell below what milestone for the first time since records began in 1899?
society.fact: About 686,000 babies were born to Japanese nationals in 2024; the first dip below 800,000 had come only two years earlier, in 2022.

society.q: In 2024, the yen fell to its weakest level against the US dollar in about 38 years. Roughly how many yen bought one dollar at the low?
society.fact: The yen touched almost 162 per dollar in July 2024; the finance ministry spent roughly 9.8 trillion yen on currency intervention in April and May alone.

society.q: In 2025, the price of which staple roughly doubled in Japan, prompting the government to release emergency stockpiles?
society.fact: A 5 kg bag passed 4,000 yen in supermarkets; agriculture minister Taku Eto resigned in May 2025 after joking that he never had to buy rice.

society.q: What Japanese term describes death from overwork, a problem that prompted legal caps on overtime from 2019?
society.fact: The 2019 work-style reform law generally capped overtime at 45 hours a month and 360 a year; the limits were extended to doctors only in April 2024.

society.q: How many foreign visitors came to Japan in 2024, a record year for tourism?
society.fact: The weak yen fuelled the boom; to tackle overcrowding, Mount Fuji's Yamanashi trail introduced a 2,000-yen fee and a daily cap of 4,000 climbers in 2024.

society.q: Which Japanese term describes people who withdraw from society and rarely leave home, estimated by a 2023 government survey at about 1.5 million?
society.fact: The Cabinet Office survey estimated 1.46 million people aged 15 to 64 were affected; around a fifth cited the pandemic as a trigger.

society.q: In 2024, people aged 65 and over made up roughly what share of Japan's population, a record high?
society.fact: Japan counted more than 95,000 centenarians in 2024, and people aged 80 or over passed 10% of the population for the first time in 2023.

society.q: What is the name of Japan's annual spring wage negotiations, which produced the biggest pay rises in over 30 years in 2024?
society.fact: The Rengo union federation reported average rises of 5.1% in 2024 and 5.25% in 2025, the highest since 1991, after decades of flat wages.

society.q: Japan's core consumer inflation averaged roughly what in 2023, the highest in about four decades after years near zero?
society.fact: Core prices (excluding fresh food) rose 3.1% in 2023, the fastest since 1982; real wages still fell for most of the year because pay lagged prices.

society.q: In December 2024, which Japanese public body announced a four-day working week option for its staff from 2025, to help parents?
society.fact: Governor Yuriko Koike framed it as support for families; Japan's total fertility rate fell to a record low of 1.15 in 2024.

society.q: A law in force from April 2021 asks Japanese companies to make efforts to let employees keep working until what age?
society.fact: Firms were already required to secure employment until 65; Japan's public pension can be claimed anywhere between 60 and 75, with larger payments for waiting.

society.q: Foreign residents in Japan reached a record of roughly how many at the end of 2024?
society.fact: The largest groups were from China, Vietnam and South Korea; foreign residents made up about 3% of the population, up from 2.9 million in 2019.

society.q: From 2022, Japan required companies with more than 300 employees to publish what figure?
society.fact: Japan's gender wage gap of around 21% was among the widest in the OECD; full-time women earned roughly three-quarters of men's pay in 2023.

society.q: Roughly what share of Japan's workers were in non-regular jobs such as part-time or contract work in 2023?
society.fact: More than half of working women held non-regular jobs; the share of all workers in such jobs had been about 20% in 1990.

society.q: From January 2022, Japan's government paid subsidies to wholesalers to hold down the retail price of what?
society.fact: The subsidy started at 5 yen a litre and was extended repeatedly as oil prices and the weak yen bit; subsidies on electricity and gas bills followed in 2023.

society.q: In 2023, the average price of a new flat in Tokyo's 23 wards exceeded what milestone for the first time?
society.fact: The average was about 115 million yen, up nearly 40% in a year, driven by central-Tokyo luxury projects and rising construction costs.

society.q: In which year did Japan's national average minimum wage first exceed 1,000 yen an hour?
society.fact: The average reached 1,004 yen in October 2023 and 1,055 yen in 2024; minimum wages are set prefecture by prefecture, with Tokyo's the highest.

society.q: Which visa category, introduced in April 2019, opened Japan to foreign workers in sectors such as construction, farming and nursing care?
society.fact: In 2024 the government also decided to replace the much-criticised Technical Intern Training Programme with a new 'employment for skill development' scheme from 2027.

society.q: Under laws passed in 2023, Japan allowed nuclear reactors to operate beyond what previous age limit?
society.fact: Time spent offline for safety reviews no longer counts towards the limit; by the end of 2024 about 14 reactors had restarted since the 2011 Fukushima disaster.

society.q: In January 2024, Japan expanded which tax-free investment account scheme to encourage households to move savings into shares?
society.fact: The annual limit rose to 3.6 million yen with a lifetime cap of 18 million; Japanese households had kept over half their financial assets in cash and deposits.

society.q: What popular scheme lets Japanese taxpayers redirect part of their taxes to a chosen municipality in return for gifts such as beef or crab?
society.fact: 'Hometown tax' donations passed 1 trillion yen in fiscal 2023 for the first time; big cities such as Tokyo's wards complain of losing tax revenue to rural towns.

society.q: What is the name of Japan's national ID card, which the government promoted with up to 20,000 yen in shopping points per person?
society.fact: Paper health-insurance cards stopped being issued in December 2024 in favour of the My Number card, despite data-linkage errors reported in 2023.

society.q: Japan's 2023 housing survey counted roughly how many empty homes, known as 'akiya'?
society.fact: Empty homes made up a record 13.8% of all housing; a 2023 law let authorities raise property tax on badly maintained vacant houses.

general.q: What is Japan's highest mountain?
general.fact: Mount Fuji rises 3,776 metres and was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2013 as a cultural site, honouring its role in art and worship.

general.q: Which is the largest of Japan's main islands?
general.fact: Honshu is the seventh-largest island in the world and home to Tokyo, Osaka and Kyoto.

general.q: Alongside kanji, which two syllabaries are used to write Japanese?
general.fact: Hiragana and katakana each have 46 basic characters, while Japan's official list of everyday-use kanji contains 2,136 characters.

general.q: The Japanese name for Japan, 'Nihon' or 'Nippon', means roughly what?
general.fact: The name is why Japan is called the 'Land of the Rising Sun', and the red disc on its flag represents the sun.

general.q: What is the highest rank in professional sumo wrestling?
general.fact: Yokozuna means 'horizontal rope', after the thick white braided rope these grand champions wear during their ring-entering ceremony.

general.q: Which fish may only be prepared by specially licensed chefs in Japan because parts of it are deadly poisonous?
general.fact: Fugu contains tetrodotoxin, a nerve poison far more potent than cyanide, so chefs train for years to remove the toxic organs safely.

general.q: What is Japan's largest freshwater lake?
general.fact: Lake Biwa in Shiga Prefecture is one of the world's oldest lakes, around 4 million years old, and supplies water to millions in the Kansai region.

general.q: How many prefectures is Japan divided into?
general.fact: The 47 comprise one metropolis (Tokyo), one circuit (Hokkaido), two urban prefectures (Osaka and Kyoto) and 43 other prefectures.

general.q: What is the capital city of Okinawa Prefecture?
general.fact: Naha is home to Shuri Castle, once the royal seat of the Ryukyu Kingdom, which ruled the islands before they became part of Japan.

general.q: Which Tokyo railway station is recognised by Guinness World Records as the world's busiest by passenger numbers?
general.fact: Shinjuku Station handles roughly 3.5 million passengers a day in normal times and has around 200 exits.

general.q: What is the currency of Japan?
general.fact: Yen means 'round' in Japanese; the currency was introduced by the Meiji government in 1871.

general.q: Hanami parties in spring celebrate the blooming of which flower?
general.fact: Japan's weather agency tracks the 'cherry blossom front' as blooms move north each year, from Okinawa in January to Hokkaido in May.

general.q: What is the name of Japan's traditional wrapped robe with wide sleeves?
general.fact: A lighter cotton kimono called a yukata is worn at summer festivals and is often provided to guests at hot-spring inns.

general.q: Which Japanese martial art's name means 'the gentle way'?
general.fact: Judo was founded by Jigoro Kano in 1882 and made its Olympic debut at the 1964 Tokyo Games.

general.q: Which of Japan's main islands is home to the Sapporo Snow Festival?
general.fact: The Sapporo Snow Festival began in 1950, when local high school students built six snow statues in Odori Park.

general.q: What are Japan's natural hot-spring baths called?
general.fact: At Jigokudani in Nagano, wild Japanese macaques, known as snow monkeys, famously bathe in hot springs during the winter.

general.q: Which Shinto shrine on an island near Hiroshima is famous for a torii gate that seems to float at high tide?
general.fact: At high tide the great torii appears to float on the sea; at low tide visitors can walk out across the sand to touch it.

general.q: Which Kyoto shrine is famous for tunnels formed by thousands of orange torii gates?
general.fact: Fushimi Inari honours Inari, the god of rice, and each gate is donated by a business or person whose name is inscribed on the back.

general.q: What is the name of Japan's top professional football league?
general.fact: The J.League kicked off in 1993 with ten clubs; Brazilian star Zico played for Kashima Antlers in its early seasons.

general.q: Which seaweed, sold in thin dried sheets, is used to wrap sushi rolls?
general.fact: Nori farming took off after British scientist Kathleen Drew-Baker revealed the seaweed's life cycle in 1949; Japanese farmers honour her as 'Mother of the Sea'.

general.q: Which strait between Honshu and Hokkaido is crossed by the Seikan Tunnel?
general.fact: The Seikan Tunnel, opened in 1988, is about 54 km long, with roughly 23 km running beneath the seabed.

general.q: What is Japan's second-highest mountain, after Mount Fuji?
general.fact: Kita-dake rises 3,193 metres in the Southern Alps of Yamanashi Prefecture and is home to a flower found nowhere else, the Kitadake-so.

general.q: What is the name of the Indigenous people of Hokkaido, recognised in a 2019 law?
general.fact: Upopoy, the National Ainu Museum and Park, opened in 2020 on the shore of Lake Poroto in Shiraoi, Hokkaido.

general.q: Which Japanese city earned the nickname 'the nation's kitchen' as the hub of the Edo-period rice trade?
general.fact: Osaka is also famous for 'kuidaore', a local motto meaning roughly 'eat until you drop'.

general.q: What is the deepest lake in Japan?
general.fact: Lake Tazawa in Akita Prefecture is about 423 metres deep, and its clear blue water does not freeze even in the region's snowy winters.
